title: Generic Classes: Building Type-Safe Containers
summary: Create generic classes: type parameter naming conventions (<T>, <E>, <K, V>), instantiating generic types, and type-safe Box and Pair classes.
learningObjectives: Declare custom generic classes with single and multiple formal type parameters: Box<T>, Pair<K, V>
Apply standard Java type parameter naming conventions: E, K, V, T, U, N
Leverage the Diamond operator (<>) for clean, type-inferred constructor invocations
Understand why static fields and methods cannot reference class-level type parameters
expectedOutcomes: Ability to architect reusable, strongly typed container classes and data structures
Understanding of JVM class loading vs generic instantiation boundaries

activities.title: Practical Context: Standardized Shipping Container Specifications

analogy.headline: Practical Context: Standardized Shipping Container Specifications
analogy.story:
Consider intermodal shipping containers transported by cargo ships and freight trains. A container's structural chassis is universal (corner castings, steel doors, standardized dimensions). However, each container is designated for a specific cargo type: RefrigeratedContainer<PerishableProduce>, LiquidTankContainer<Petroleum>, or SecureContainer<Electronics>.

The container hardware itself does not need to be redesigned from scratch for every new product. Instead, the container framework is parameterizable, enforcing strict safety rules on what goes inside while sharing identical locking and hoisting mechanisms across all freight operations.
analogy.keyTakeaway: A generic class defines a reusable architectural blueprint where the concrete payload type is decoupled and parameterized at instantiation time.

activities.title: Generic Class Architecture: Declaration, Naming, and Static Boundaries

keyTakeaways: A generic class is declared with type parameters following class name: class Box<T> { ... }
Standard naming conventions: E (element), K (key), V (value), T (type), N (number), S/U/V (2nd/3rd types)
Java 7+ Diamond operator (<>) enables compiler type inference during constructor calls
Static members cannot access class type parameters because static fields/methods belong to the class, not instances

activities.title: Immutable Pair Container Implementation
activities.description: Trace the construction and type inference of a two-parameter generic container Pair<K, V>.

steps.description: Declare Pair with formal parameters <A, B>. Fields are declared final to enforce immutability.
Instantiate Pair using diamond syntax new Pair<>('Alice', 98). The compiler infers A as String and B as Integer.
Access fields via getters. studentGrade.getFirst() returns String directly with no casting.

questions.question: Why is 'private static T instance;' not permitted inside a generic class 'public class Holder<T>'?
options: Because static variables cannot be private
Because static fields belong to the raw loaded class and are shared across all instantiations regardless of their type arguments
Because Java does not support static variables inside classes
questions.explanation: At runtime, Holder.class is loaded once by the JVM. If a static field referenced T, it would be impossible to know what type it should be if one instance is Holder<String> and another is Holder<Integer>.

questions.question: What is the primary function of the diamond operator (<>) introduced in Java 7?
options: It forces the JVM to optimize garbage collection for generic objects
It allows the compiler to automatically infer type arguments for generic constructors from the variable declaration context
It permits primitive types in generics like List<int>
It bypasses type erasure at runtime
questions.explanation: The diamond operator (<>) enables constructor type inference: instead of writing 'new Box<String>()', you write 'new Box<>()', reducing boilerplate while preserving complete compile-time type safety.

activities.title: Senior Engineer Interview: Creating Generic Instances

qaList.question: Why cannot a generic class instantiate its type parameter directly using 'new T()' or 'new T[10]', and how do production frameworks solve this?
qaList.answer:
A generic class cannot instantiate 'new T()' or 'new T[10]' because of Java's Type Erasure. At compile time, type parameter T is erased to Object (or its bound). The JVM bytecode instructions 'new' and 'anewarray' require an explicit reified runtime class token to know how many bytes to allocate. Because T does not exist at runtime, the compiler cannot generate the appropriate instantiation bytecode.

Production frameworks solve this using Type Tokens: pass 'Class<T> clazz' into the constructor and invoke reflection: 'clazz.getDeclaredConstructor().newInstance()'. For arrays, use 'Array.newInstance(clazz, capacity)' with an explicit cast '(T[]) Array.newInstance(clazz, capacity)'.

activities.title: Self-Evaluation Checklist
checklist: I can declare custom generic classes with single and multiple type parameters
I follow standard naming conventions: E, K, V, T, U, N
I understand why static fields and methods cannot reference class-level type parameters

practiceProblems.title: Generic Array-Backed LIFO Stack
practiceProblems.problemStatement: Implement a generic stack class GenericStack<T> with push(T item), pop(), peek(), and isEmpty() methods, managing an internal Object[] array and casting safely upon retrieval.

practiceProblems.title: Custom Type-Safe Maybe<T> Monad
practiceProblems.problemStatement: Implement a simplified custom Maybe<T> container with static factory methods Maybe.of(T value) and Maybe.empty(), plus methods isPresent(), get(), and orElse(T fallback).

practiceProblems.title: Three-Element Generic Tuple (Triplet)
practiceProblems.problemStatement: Implement an immutable Triplet<A, B, C> class that stores three distinct types and provides getters getFirst(), getSecond(), and getThird().

practiceProblems.title: Generic Circular Ring Buffer
practiceProblems.problemStatement: Implement a generic RingBuffer<T> with fixed capacity that overwrites the oldest element when full. Implement offer(T item), poll(), and size().

testCases.input: offer(1), offer(2), offer(3), offer(4), poll(), poll(), poll()

practiceProblems.title: Type-Safe Value Swapper
practiceProblems.problemStatement: Implement a class Holder<T> that holds a single value. Add a method swap(Holder<T> other) that swaps the values stored inside two holders of the same type.
